children.text: A cluster of around 24 limestone islands off San Agustin in Surigao del Sur. Green islands rise from an emerald sea, and pure white sandbars appear at low tide, earning the group the nickname "the El Nido of Mindanao" — though far fewer tourists come here, so you can still enjoy quiet island hopping.

The Britania Islands (officially the Britania Group of Islands) are a cluster of around 24 small islands scattered off Britania barangay in San Agustin, Surigao del Sur, in northeastern Mindanao. Most of the islands are limestone covered in dense tropical forest, and the water between them shifts from jade to deep turquoise depending on the depth. Photos alone bring to mind El Nido or Coron in Palawan, which is why locals sometimes call the group "the El Nido of Mindanao."

The islands' biggest draw is how quiet they are. The eastern Mindanao coast facing the Pacific has poor transport links and almost no large resorts, so even in peak season it isn't unusual to have an entire island to yourselves. The long white beach of Hagonoy Island, the sandbar of Naked Island that only appears at low tide, and the cliff viewpoint of Boslon Island can all be covered in a single day on one bangka.
The islands sit within
5–20 minutes

of each other by bangka from the coast, so there's little risk of seasickness, and each island has its own character. Long sandy beaches, cliffs and rock outcrops, and uninhabited islets appear in turn, so the scenery never grows dull even on a single day tour. The surrounding sea is relatively calm, since the Pacific swell is blocked by the islands, so families new to the water can swim safely in the shallows too.

The community runs tourism together, so tour boats, entrance fees, and cottage rentals are all arranged through the Britania tourism office. Instead of fancy facilities, all you'll find are simple bungalows and grilled seafood — but that's exactly why you can feel what a rural Philippine sea used to look like.

The islands suit travelers tired of crowded destinations, drone and landscape photographers, and anyone planning a road trip along the eastern Mindanao coast toward Butuan or Tandag. They may feel inconvenient, though, for those who want comfortable resorts and a wide choice of restaurants.
Rent a bangka at the tourism office and spend
3–5 hours
visiting the main islands, including Hagonoy, Naked, and Boslon. About 10 people typically share a boat, so the cost per person drops sharply the more people you have.

The best-known island in the group, with a long, fine white beach and shallow water good for swimming and picnic lunches. Renting a cottage and eating food you've brought along is the local way to spend half a day here.
A treeless white sandbar that appears or disappears depending on the tide. You'll need to time your visit for low tide to get photos that look like you're standing in the middle of the open sea.
A spot known for its striking view of green peaks layered between the islands. A short climb up leads to a lookout over the whole group, making it a favorite for once-in-a-lifetime photos.
You can spot tropical fish over the shallow coral beds around the islands. Rental gear isn't always plentiful, so it's best to bring your own mask and snorkel.

Buy fish, squid, or shellfish at the San Agustin market or near the pier and bring them to the island — the boatman or cottage caretaker will often grill them for you. It's good manners to ask in advance and offer a small tip.
After the tour, watch the sun set beyond the islands and the fishing boats return to shore. With few tourists around, you can fully take in a quiet rural evening.
Take a bus or van from Butuan Airport or downtown toward Tandag and travel to the San Agustin–Britania crossing (about
4–5 hours
Take a tricycle to the tourism office, check in at your accommodation, and have lunch.
Start your afternoon of island hopping. Swim and relax on Hagonoy Island, then take in the viewpoint on Boslon Island.
Watch the sunset from the pier and have a seafood dinner near your accommodation.
Check the tide schedule and revisit Naked Island's sandbar and nearby snorkeling spots early in the morning — the morning light is best for photos.
Return to your accommodation to shower and check out.
Onward — head back to Butuan, or continue your trip north toward Tandag or south toward Bislig (Tinuy-an Falls).
A direct flight from Manila to Butuan Airport (BXU) takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
. One-way fares run around
depending on the season. From Cebu to Butuan takes about
1 hour
. Tandag Airport (TDG) only has occasional small-plane flights, so check whether it's operating before you leave.
From Butuan Airport, head to downtown or the bus terminal, then take a bus or van bound for Tandag and ask to be dropped at "Britania Crossing" or "Salvacion." The trip takes about
4–5 hours
, and the fare is around
. From Davao, the usual route is via San Francisco in Agusan del Sur, transferring to a Tandag-bound bus, which takes about
7–9 hours
From the highway crossing, it's a short tricycle ride to the tourism office and pier, costing around
. Island-hopping bangkas are assigned at the tourism office, at around
per boat (for 10–15 people). If your group is small, it's worth asking the office about sharing a boat with other travelers.
From Cebu, flying into Butuan or Surigao City (SUG) is fastest. There's also an overnight ferry between Cebu and Surigao, but from Surigao City to Britania is another bus ride of about
5–6 hours
, which is less convenient than going via Butuan. If you're combining this with a Siargao trip, routing through Surigao City and down through Butuan keeps your travel moving in one direction.
Surigao del Sur faces the Pacific directly on Mindanao's east coast, so its weather differs from the western Philippines. There's no clear dry season and rain falls year-round, but from
November
to
February
the northeast monsoon (Amihan) brings the heaviest rain and highest waves, and island-hopping tours are often canceled during this period.
The best time to visit is from
April
to
September
, when the sea is calm and the sunlight brings out the clearest water colors. From July to
September
, though, winds can pick up from the indirect effect of typhoons passing over the northern Philippines, so check the forecast before you leave.
The timing of Naked Island's sandbar depends on the tide, so it's best to check a tide table before visiting and coordinate timing with your boatman. During Holy Week (the week before Easter) and the
May
holidays, visits from nearby residents increase and cottages can get crowded.

A handful of small, family-run beach resorts and bungalows sit near the Britania pier and along the coastal road. Fan rooms run about
a night, and air-conditioned rooms about

; many places have no hot water or Wi-Fi. Power supply isn't very reliable either, so bring plenty of portable battery packs. If you'd rather stay somewhere more comfortable, you can also base yourself in Tandag to the north (about
1 hour
) or Bislig to the south and visit for the day.

Seafood is the clear standout. Fresh fish tossed with vinegar, ginger, and chili (kinilaw), charcoal-grilled fish (sinugba), and tangy sinigang soup are all common. Since there aren't many restaurants, most visitors either pre-order meals through their accommodation or buy ingredients at the San Agustin market and ask someone to cook them. Islands have almost no shops, so be sure to bring your own water and snacks. In the coastal towns of Surigao del Sur, you can buy tuna, mackerel tuna, and crab cheaply at the early-morning fish market, and in the evening try grilled chicken or pork skewers from roadside barbecue stalls for around
. Heading into Tandag town opens up more choices, including fast-food chains and Filipino home-style eateries (carinderias).
San Agustin has almost no ATMs. Withdraw enough cash in Butuan or Tandag to cover tour costs and accommodation.
Phone signal is mostly limited to the area around the pier and often drops out on the islands. It helps to carry both a Smart and a Globe SIM card.
Bangka fares are set per boat, so with only 2–4 people the cost per person rises quickly. Visiting on a weekend gives you more chances to share a boat with other travelers.
The islands offer little shade. Bring a wide-brimmed hat, a rash guard, and reef-safe sunscreen.
A dry bag and water shoes make boarding the bangka and walking the sandbars much easier.
The water shows its clearest color for photos between
8 and 10 a.m.
. If you fly a drone, be considerate of local residents' and other visitors' privacy.
If you're doing an east-coast road trip, it's efficient to combine this with Enchanted River (Hinatuan) or Tinuy-an Falls (Bislig) for a 3–4 day itinerary.
From
November to February
, rough seas sometimes lead the coast guard to ban small-boat travel for the day. Tours are canceled on such days, so build some slack into your schedule.

Some inland mountainous parts of Surigao del Sur have reported security concerns. Stick to the main coastal roads and tourist areas, and avoid long-distance travel late at night. Check your home country's travel advisory for the latest guidance before you go.
Ask for a life vest when boarding a bangka, and don't board a boat that's over its passenger limit.
Stepping on coral or taking shells and coral home is prohibited. Always take your trash back with you.
The islands have almost no drinking water, shops, or first-aid facilities. Bring all the water, snacks, and basic medicine you'll need before you set out.
About
2–3 hours
by car to Hinatuan in the south, a mysterious spot famed for its blue river of unknown depth.
About
3–4 hours
by car to Bislig in the south, a wide, tiered waterfall known as the "Niagara of the Philippines."
Reached by boat via Butuan and Surigao, an island known as the surfing capital of the Philippines.
About
1 hour
by car to the north, the provincial capital of Surigao del Sur, with a wider range of accommodation and restaurants.
